grammar.title: Present simple and continuous
points: Use the present simple for habits, routines and facts: 'My cousin plays basketball on Saturdays.' 'Cats hate water.'
With he, she and it add -s or -es (goes, watches, studies). Use don't / doesn't for negatives and do / does for questions: 'Does Leo like pizza?'
Make the present continuous with am / is / are + verb-ing. Use it for things happening now or around now: 'Shh, the baby is sleeping.'
The present continuous is also for temporary situations and for fixed future plans: 'We're visiting Grandma on Sunday.'
Verbs of liking, thinking and needing (like, love, hate, know, want, need, understand) normally stay in the present simple: 'I need a pen', not 'I'm needing a pen'.
Frequency adverbs (always, usually, often, sometimes, never) go with the present simple; now, at the moment and today often go with the continuous.

grammar.title: Past simple
points: Regular verbs add -ed (walked). Verbs ending in -e add only -d (danced); consonant + y changes to -ied (carried); a short vowel + consonant doubles the consonant (stopped).
Many common verbs are irregular and you have to learn them: go - went, buy - bought, see - saw, take - took.
The form is the same for every person: 'I arrived late and they arrived late too.'
Negatives use didn't + infinitive and questions use did + subject + infinitive: 'We didn't win.' 'Did you call her?'
The verb be is different: was / were, wasn't / weren't, with no did: 'Were you at home?' 'It wasn't funny.'
Use the past simple for finished actions and situations, often with a time expression: yesterday, last week, two days ago, in 2019.

grammar.title: Comparatives and superlatives
points: Short adjectives: add -er / the -est (cheap, cheaper, the cheapest). After -e add only -r / -st (large, larger). After one vowel + one consonant, double the consonant (hot, hotter, the hottest).
Two-syllable adjectives ending in -y change y to i: easy, easier, the easiest.
Longer adjectives use more / the most: 'Maths is more difficult than art.' 'It's the most exciting game I know.'
Irregular forms: good - better - the best; bad - worse - the worst.
Use than after a comparative: 'My bike is faster than yours.' Use not as + adjective + as to say something is less: 'Tea isn't as strong as coffee.'
Superlatives need the, and often in or of: 'the tallest boy in the class', 'the best day of my life'.

grammar.title: Past continuous
points: Form: was / were + verb-ing. 'I was reading.' 'They were laughing.'
Negative: wasn't / weren't + -ing. Questions: Was / Were + subject + -ing? 'Were you listening?' Short answers: 'Yes, I was.' / 'No, we weren't.'
Use it for an action in progress at a moment in the past: 'At nine o'clock last night we were having dinner.'
Use it to describe the background scene of a story: 'The sun was shining and people were sitting outside.'
Spelling of -ing: drop a final -e (make - making) and double the consonant after a short vowel (sit - sitting, run - running).

grammar.title: Past simple and continuous
points: Past continuous = a longer action in progress in the past. Past simple = a short, finished action.
Used together, the long action (continuous) is interrupted by the short one (simple): 'I was having a shower when the phone rang.'
when usually introduces the past simple action; while usually introduces the past continuous action: 'While we were walking home, it started to rain.'
Two past simple verbs mean one action happened after the other: 'When the bell rang, everybody left.'
State verbs such as know, like, want and believe are not normally used in the continuous: 'I knew the answer', not 'I was knowing the answer'.

grammar.title: some/any, much/many, a lot of, a few / a little
points: some: positive sentences, with plural and uncountable nouns ('some apples', 'some rice'). any: negatives and most questions ('We haven't got any eggs.' 'Is there any juice?').
a lot of = a large amount. It works with countable and uncountable nouns in all kinds of sentence: 'She has a lot of friends and a lot of energy.'
many + plural countable nouns and much + uncountable nouns, mostly in questions and negatives: 'How many chairs are there?' 'There isn't much time.'
a few + plural countable nouns and a little + uncountable nouns = a small amount, in positive sentences and questions: 'a few coins', 'a little salt'.
Uncountable nouns (money, water, homework, furniture, advice, bread) have no plural and take a singular verb: 'The homework is easy.'

grammar.title: have to and must; should
points: have to + infinitive = it is necessary, often because of a rule. It changes form: has to, had to. 'Nurses often have to work at night.'
must + infinitive (no to, no -s) also means it is necessary, often in the speaker's opinion. It has no past form: use had to. 'I must phone Gran.'
mustn't = it is not allowed: 'You mustn't run in the corridor.'
don't / doesn't have to = it isn't necessary; you can choose: 'We don't have to get up early on Sunday.'
should / shouldn't + infinitive gives advice or an opinion: 'You should drink more water.' 'He shouldn't stay up so late.' Question: 'Should I tell her?'

grammar.title: Future: be going to and present continuous
points: Use the present continuous for definite arrangements, usually with a time, a place or other people: 'We're meeting Carla at six.'
Use be going to + infinitive for intentions, things you have decided to do: 'I'm going to learn the guitar this year.'
be going to is also for predictions when you can see the evidence now: 'Watch out! That glass is going to fall.'
Form: am / is / are (not) + going to + verb. Questions: 'Are you going to tell him?' Short answers: 'Yes, I am.' / 'No, I'm not.'
A present continuous sentence about the future normally needs a future time expression (tonight, on Friday, next week) or a clear context.

grammar.title: Present perfect
points: Form: have / has + past participle. 'I've finished.' 'She hasn't arrived.' 'Have they eaten?'
Regular past participles end in -ed, the same as the past simple. Irregular ones must be learned: see - saw - seen, write - wrote - written, do - did - done.
Use it for past actions that are connected to now, when the exact time is not said: 'I've lost my keys' (= I can't find them now).
Use ever in questions and never in statements about life experience: 'Have you ever ridden a horse?' 'I've never tried sushi.' Short answers: 'Yes, I have.' / 'No, I haven't.'
been or gone? 'She's been to London' = she went and came back. 'She's gone to London' = she is there now.

grammar.title: Present perfect and past simple; How long? and for/since
points: Present perfect: experiences in your life up to now, with no finished time mentioned. 'I've visited Rome.'
Past simple: when you say exactly when, with finished time words such as yesterday, last year, in 2020, two days ago. 'I visited Rome last summer.'
Conversations often start in the present perfect and continue in the past simple for the details: 'Have you ever been camping?' 'Yes, we went to the Pyrenees in July.'
How long + present perfect asks about something that started in the past and still continues: 'How long have you lived here?'
for + a period of time (for two hours, for six months, for ages); since + the starting point (since Monday, since 2019, since I was a child).

grammar.title: will and be going to
points: will / won't + infinitive is for general predictions and opinions about the future, often after I think, I'm sure or probably: 'I think robots will do most jobs.'

be going to is for plans you decided before speaking: 'I'm going to visit my aunt on Saturday. I've already told her.'
be going to is also for predictions based on something you can see now: 'He's driving too fast. He's going to crash!'
will is the same for all persons. Short forms: I'll, she'll, won't. Question: 'Will you be at home tonight?'

grammar.title: Modals of probability
points: Modal verbs of probability show how sure you are. They never change form and are followed by an infinitive without to: 'She must be at home.'
must = I'm almost certain it is true: 'You've run ten kilometres. You must be thirsty.'
might / could = it is possible, but I'm not sure: 'Take an umbrella. It might rain.' 'This could be the right street.'
can't = I'm almost certain it is NOT true: 'That can't be Leo - he's in France this week.' Don't use mustn't for this meaning.
might not = perhaps not: 'She might not come to the party.'

grammar.title: just, already and yet
points: just, already and yet are used with the present perfect (have / has + past participle).
just = a very short time ago. It goes between have / has and the participle: 'The bus has just left.'
already = before now, or sooner than expected. It normally goes between have / has and the participle, sometimes at the end: 'I've already seen this episode.'
yet = until now. Put it at the end of negatives and questions, when you expect something to happen: 'I haven't had lunch yet.' 'Has the film started yet?'
Don't use yet in positive sentences or already in negative ones: 'I haven't finished yet', not 'I haven't already finished'.
questions: I haven't finished my project ____. (yet / already / just) | yet
'Do you want a sandwich?' 'No, thanks. I've ____ eaten.' (already / yet) | already
The floor is wet because I've ____ cleaned it. (just / yet) | just
Have you done the washing-up ____? (yet / just / already) | yet
Put 'just' in the right place: She has arrived. | She has just arrived.
Put 'yet' in the right place: They haven't called. | They haven't called yet.
Put 'already' before the main verb: We have bought the tickets. | We have already bought the tickets.
Correct it: I haven't already eaten. | I haven't eaten yet.
Correct it: He has just go out. | He has just gone out.
It's only ten o'clock and she has ____ done all her work! (already / yet) | already
'Is Tom here?' 'No, he's ____ left. You missed him by a minute.' (just / yet) | just
Hurry up! The match ____ (just / start). | has just started

grammar.title: Relative clauses
points: A relative clause tells us which person, thing or place we mean: 'The girl who sits next to me is from Peru.'
Use who or that for people: 'a doctor who / that works with children'. Use which or that for things: 'the bus which / that goes to the centre'.
Use where for places: 'This is the café where we had breakfast.'
The relative pronoun can be the subject of its clause ('the boy who won the race') or the object ('the boy who I met yesterday').
Don't add an extra pronoun: 'the film that I saw', not 'the film that I saw it'.
questions: She's the teacher ____ helped me. (who / which / where) | who
This is the phone ____ I bought yesterday. (who / which / where) | which
That's the park ____ we play football. (who / which / where) | where
Correct it: That's the book that I read it. | That's the book that I read.
A baker is a person ____ makes bread. (who / which) | who
A fridge is a machine ____ keeps food cold. (who / which) | which
Join with 'where': That's the hotel. We stayed there. = That's the hotel ____. | where we stayed
Which word can replace 'who'? The boy who called you is my cousin. (that / which / where) | that
Is this the shop ____ you lost your wallet? (which / where / who) | where
Correct it: She's the girl who she won. | She's the girl who won.
I like films ____ make me laugh. (who / that / where) | that
Join with 'who': I have a friend. He speaks Chinese. = I have a friend ____. | who speaks Chinese

grammar.title: Present simple passive
points: Form: am / is / are + past participle. 'Rice is grown in Asia.' 'These cars are made in Germany.'
Negative: isn't / aren't + participle. Question: Is / Are + subject + participle? 'Is French spoken in Canada?'
Use the passive when the action or the object is more important than who does it, or when we don't know who does it: 'The rubbish is collected on Mondays.'
The object of an active sentence becomes the subject of the passive one: 'People speak Spanish here.' - 'Spanish is spoken here.'
Add by + person or thing only when it matters who does the action: 'The school website is updated by the students.'
questions: Cheese ____ (make) from milk. | is made
Millions of emails ____ (send) every minute. | are sent

grammar.title: Zero and first conditional
points: Conditional sentences have an if-clause (the condition) and a result clause. Either can come first; use a comma when the if-clause is first.
Zero conditional: if + present simple, present simple. It is for things that are always true: 'If you mix blue and yellow, you get green.'
First conditional: if + present simple, will / won't + infinitive. It is for a possible future situation: 'If it rains tomorrow, we'll stay in.'
Never put will in the if-clause: 'If I see her, I'll tell her', not 'If I will see her'.
unless = if ... not: 'We'll miss the bus unless we run.' Use when if you are sure it will happen, and if when you are not sure: 'When I get home, I'll call you.'
questions: If you heat ice, it ____ (melt). | melts
If it rains tomorrow, we ____ (stay) at home. | will stay
If she ____ (study) hard, she'll pass the exam. | studies
Correct it: If it will rain, we'll stay. | If it rains, we'll stay.
You won't pass ____ you study. (if / unless) | unless
Plants die if they ____ (not / get) water. | don't get

Unless it ____ (stop) raining, we won't play. | stops

grammar.title: Reported commands
points: To report an order, a request or advice, use: reporting verb + person + to + infinitive. 'Sit down!' - 'The teacher told us to sit down.'
For negatives use not to + infinitive: 'Don't shout!' - 'She told them not to shout.'
Common reporting verbs: tell (orders), ask (polite requests), advise (advice), and also warn, remind, persuade, encourage and convince.
You can't use say in this pattern: 'He told me to wait', not 'He said me to wait'.
Pronouns and possessives change to fit the new speaker: 'Open your books.' - 'She told us to open our books.'
questions: 'Close the window.' - He told me ____ the window. | to close
'Don't be late.' - Mum told us ____ late. | not to be
'Please help me.' - She ____ me to help her. (said / asked) | asked

grammar.title: Second conditional
points: Form: if + past simple, would / wouldn't + infinitive. 'If I had a boat, I would sail around the world.'
Use it for imaginary, unreal or unlikely situations in the present or future. It does not talk about the past.
Either clause can come first; use a comma when the if-clause is first. The short form of would is 'd: 'I'd buy it if it was cheaper.'
After I, he, she and it you can use were instead of was, especially to give advice: 'If I were you, I'd say sorry.'
Never put would in the if-clause: 'If I knew', not 'If I would know'. Question: 'What would you do if you saw a ghost?'

grammar.title: Reported speech
points: When you report what someone said, the verb usually moves one step back into the past: present simple - past simple; present continuous - past continuous; will - would; can - could.
'I like jazz,' said Ben. - 'Ben said (that) he liked jazz.' The word that is optional.
Pronouns and possessives change to fit the situation: 'I'll call my mum,' said Eva. - 'Eva said she would call her mum.'
say or tell? say + what was said: 'He said he was tired.' tell + person + what was said: 'He told me he was tired.'
questions: 'I live in Leeds,' said Tom. - Tom said he ____ in Leeds. | lived

grammar.title: Past simple passive
points: Form: was / were + past participle. 'The bridge was built in 1900.' 'The windows were broken.'
Negative: wasn't / weren't + participle. Question: Was / Were + subject + participle? 'Was the thief caught?'
Use it when the action is more important than the person who did it, or when we don't know who did it: 'My bike was stolen last night.'
To say who or what did the action, use by: 'The Mona Lisa was painted by Leonardo da Vinci.'
From active to passive, the object becomes the subject: 'Someone found the keys.' - 'The keys were found.'
questions: The first iPhone ____ (sell) in 2007. | was sold
These pyramids ____ (build) thousands of years ago. | were built
The window ____ (not / break) by the children. | wasn't broken
____ the emails sent yesterday? (Was / Were / Did) | Were

Make it passive: Someone stole my wallet. = My wallet ____. | was stolen
Make it passive: They found the paintings in a garage. = The paintings ____ in a garage. | were found
When ____ this school opened? (was / were / did) | was
Make it active: The goal was scored by Alba. = Alba ____ the goal. | scored
